plot: You decide to stay up all night. Cortez cancels the sleep shift, and Addy (adenosine) piles into the brain's slow-down chairs while coffee only blocks them. Gus gets flooded by ghrelin, the brain's night cleanup crew never shows, Beat nods off mid-call, reaction time slides to drunk-driving levels, cortisol fakes a second wind, and only sleep finally clears Addy out. Tease: your first gym day in a year.

script.title: Inside You When You Pull an All-Nighter

beats.title: Inside You When You Pull an All-Nighter

beats.say: Code red! He's staying up ALL night. The sleep shift is canceled!
Canceled?! My nightly blood pressure break was on the schedule!
beats.label: Blood pressure: usually dips 10 to 20% in sleep

beats.say: So the kitchen stays open? Perfect. I never close anyway.
Night shift? Finally, company. I brought snacks. Healthy ones.
I'll file this under bad ideas. Tonight's total: many.
Boss, I have forty calls waiting, and every one says tired.
Here's the plan. We follow one troublemaker until sunrise.
Hi! I'm Addy. Short for adenosine. Think of me as brain-work leftovers.
beats.label: Adenosine: builds up while you're awake

beats.say: Cells burn fuel called ATP. I'm what gets left behind.
beats.label: ATP: the fuel your cells burn

beats.say: Every awake hour, more Addys show up. We call that sleep pressure.
And I'm just getting started! Wait until you meet my cousins!
Midnight. Report. Why do my neurons feel like wet laundry?
How many chairs are taken? Give me a number.
A third, maybe? It's early. I'm still stretching.
Sorry, boss. My cousins and I are sitting in the slow-down chairs.
beats.label: Adenosine receptors: chairs that slow neurons down

beats.say: Get out of those chairs! Feeling sleepy is... denied!
Cute stamp. The chairs are still taken.
Why is everybody yelling? I'm on hold with the lungs here!
Fine. Send in the coffee. Quick!
Quick note. Coffee doesn't remove Addy. It just blocks the chairs.
beats.label: Caffeine: blocks adenosine receptors

beats.say: So I'm still here. I'm just standing in the hallway.
Fine. That buys us a little time. Next problem!
Splash his face with cold water! That'll fix everything!
Brrr. Rude. Anyway, I'm still here. Hi again.
Turn up the screen. Bright light will keep him awake!
Bright screens tell your body clock it's still daytime.
beats.label: Melatonin: the body's 'it's dark' signal

beats.say: Perfect. Daytime at midnight. I love this job.
Alarm! Study says short sleep boosts my hunger hormone almost thirty percent!
beats.label: Ghrelin: the hormone that says eat

beats.say: And leptin, the I'm-full memo, dropped about eighteen percent.
beats.label: Leptin: the hormone that says full

beats.say: So now the brain wants chips, cookies, and a drive-thru.
I'm filing every receipt. They all say, bad idea.
Bad ideas taste AMAZING at two in the morning.
Cereal at two AM. It's breakfast's cousin, called regret.
Also, tired bodies handle sugar slower. I'm keeping notes.
Notes don't fill a plate, pal. Burrito order, coming right up!
A burrito at two AM is not a choice. It's a symptom.
Great. Notes. Pass the chips.
Hey, who's on cleanup tonight? My office is a mess.
While you sleep, brain fluid flushes waste out from between your cells.
beats.label: Glymphatic system: the brain's night cleanup crew

beats.say: That crew only works the sleep shift. They're not coming.
Can we hire a night crew? Somebody with a mop?
The crew clocks in when we're asleep. That's the whole deal.
Don't worry. I brought friends. Lots of friends.
In mice, gaps between brain cells grew about sixty percent in sleep.
So awake means the trash stays? Terrible office policy!
Boss, I've got a fun idea. Could we take a nap?
I tried counting sheep. They all asked for overtime.
Denied! Sleep is for people with weekends.
I'll just sit here and pile up. No rush.
Road trip! Next stop, the front office, where decisions get made.
Hurry! I can't keep this pace. No nighttime break for me!
beats.label: Heart rate: usually slows during sleep

beats.say: Sorry, Beat. I'm just a passenger. A very heavy passenger.
Beat, pick up line one. Beat? Hello? Anybody?
Huh? Oh! Sorry. The phone rang... a while ago.
Beat, one more time. Pick up the phone. Right now.
Sorry, who is this? ...Oh. Hi, boss. Where am I?
Fine, I'll read the memo. Why is the memo upside down?
The memo is fine, boss. You're the one upside down.
Attention lapses like this get more common the longer you stay awake.
That's a microsleep. The brain checks out for a few seconds.
beats.label: Microsleep: seconds when the brain checks out

beats.say: Now picture him driving. On the interstate. At seventy miles an hour.
Don't say that! Give me the reaction time report!
After 24 awake hours, you score like a point one blood alcohol.
beats.label: Reaction time: slows after long wakefulness

beats.say: The legal driving limit in most states is point oh eight.
So I'm a tipsy manager. That explains my memos.
It's four AM. Body temperature just hit its lowest point.
beats.label: Core temperature: lowest in the early morning

beats.say: Anybody else cold? I'm wearing a headset, not a jacket.
I have a clock too. Snacks at three AM confuse it.
beats.label: Circadian clock: tells organs when to work

beats.say: Cold, hungry, and tired. Honestly, my best night yet.
Look, I work nights. But even I'd call this a lot.
Come on, Liv. Stay. Let's watch the sun come up together.
Sure. I'll bring the lamp. You bring the bad decisions.
Can I borrow a blanket? Any blanket. A memo works.
Memos aren't blankets. Somebody dropped a spoon and I want to cry.
Same! Also, I'm laughing. I don't know why!
One scan study found the emotion alarm reacted sixty percent more.
beats.label: Amygdala: the brain's emotion alarm bell

beats.say: Great. So everything is either hilarious or a tragedy.
Incoming: cortisol. The body's built-in morning alarm clock.
beats.label: Cortisol: stress hormone that climbs before dawn

beats.say: Why does cortisol always show up with a megaphone?
Fine. New memo. Feeling awake is... approved!
Oh wow. I feel great! Is this a second wind?
Everybody back to work! We're basically a morning team now!
Your body clock sends a daytime signal. Alertness bounces back a little.
Don't get excited. I'm still here, and I brought my cousins.
Morning light also tells your body clock the day has started.
Then why does everyone still feel like cold oatmeal?
Because the chairs are still full, boss. I'm good at my job.
So all that yelling and stamping did nothing?
Correct. And this sunrise meeting could have been an email.
Only real sleep clears adenosine out. Coffee just hides him.
Six AM! Addy count is off the charts! Everybody brace!
I brought everyone. Even my second cousins twice removed.
Great. Now the chairs are full, and the aisles too.
Focus, people! Sunrise is in one hour. Somebody make coffee!
Coffee? We're out of coffee. We're out of everything!
Please, just sleep soon. The kitchen has nothing left to give.
My blood pressure never took its break. I'm exhausted.
Everybody listen up. Final memo of the night.
Tonight, we sleep. Early. No excuses, no extra episodes.
Aw. I get cleared out? Tell the chairs I'll miss them.
During sleep, adenosine levels drop. That's why a full night resets you.
Final tally: six stamps, one microsleep, zero rest. Filed.
From now on, the sleep shift starts at ten sharp.
Next time: your first gym day in a year. Warn the legs.

fact.title: REAL BODY NOTE
lines: Sleep clears adenosine, your sleep signal.
Awake 24 hours acts like a 0.10 BAC.

long.title: Inside You When You Pull an All-Nighter
long.description:
It's 11 PM and you said one more episode. Cortez cancels the sleep shift, Addy the sleepy molecule moves into the brain, and every organ pays for it by sunrise.
A funny, body-accurate night inside you: adenosine, the brain's missing cleanup crew, hunger hormones, microsleeps and a very fake second wind.

Real body notes (sources): StatPearls, Physiology of Sleep and Caffeine (NCBI Bookshelf); Spiegel et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 2004 (ghrelin and leptin after short sleep); Xie et al., Science, 2013 (brain cleanup during sleep, in mice); Yoo et al., Current Biology, 2007 (emotion alarm after lost sleep); Dawson and Reid, Nature, 1997 (24 hours awake vs. blood alcohol); NIH NIGMS, Circadian Rhythms; American Heart Association (nighttime blood pressure dip).
Entertainment and general education, not medical advice. Original characters, animated in Blender.
